Loader derives approval scope from attacker-supplied `?delegation` param via readApprovalDelegation, which is jwt.decode with NO signature/expiry verification (approvalDelegation.server.ts:20). A manager can forge a token {fromManagerId:<victim manager>, toManagerId:<own id>} to set scopeManagerId to any manager, then the loader returns that team's pending submitted onboarding tasks and compensation records (salary/bonus/employee PII) at lines 102-184, bypassing the direct-report scope binding present in the plain flow.

connector_approve_task trusts a client-controlled `x-workflow-connector-result` header as its only authorization gate. canAutoCompleteOnboardingTaskSafe only compares the header's actorId (attacker can set to their own id) to currentUser.id and requires actorRole==='hr_admin' (forgeable). After passing, the task is fetched by arbitrary taskId (line 219) and approved with NO check that the task's assignee is a direct report, unlike the regular approve_task path which verifies assignee.managerId===currentUser.id (line 270). Any manager can therefore approve/reject any employee's task.
An HTTP response construction serializes caught exception detail (message) without normalization, disclosing internal diagnostic information to the client.

One initial password is generated and hashed before a bulk-account loop, then assigned to multiple independently authenticating principals.

`action` completes an account-recovery/verification flow — issuing a session or writing a new password — without ever comparing the submitted proof against the stored secret. The account is selected by an attacker-supplied identifier alone, so anyone who knows the email address can take the account over. Compare the proof in constant time against the stored (hashed) value and require it to be unexpired and single-use.
